text:
ThreeRT 

 Hardware ray-traced three.js. 

 
 A real-time path tracer behind a three.js-style API. Write the scene you would write in three.js, 
 and every light in it is traced on the GPU's ray-tracing hardware, at 60 fps.
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 Website ·
 Apps ·
 Download ·
 Docs ·
 Discord ·
 X 
 

 
 
 
 ThreeRT, live on an Apple M3 Max: this repository's demos and OpenStrike, a shooter built on the engine, on its own map. 
 

 Three + RT

 Three , for the API you already know. RT , for the three things it adds:

- Ray tracing. Every light is traced: shadows, bounce light, reflections, and glowing surfaces that light the room. No shadow maps, no light probes, no lightmaps, no baking.
- Real time. 60 fps in production scenes with the camera moving: Amazon Lumberyard Bistro and Beeple's Zero-Day, on a laptop. Not a still that converges once you stop.
- Runtime. A game runtime, not only a renderer. Scene code and game logic run inside the engine, and the same file runs as plain three.js in any browser.

 Hello world looks right

Write a scene at tutorial size and leave every setting at its default.

 

 three.js, as written ThreeRT, all defaults 
 --- --- 
 

The sun through the window, the sky, the bounce light off the floor and the lamp's glow come from tracing the scene. Light is in physical units: the sun is 90,000 lux, and an emissive surface is a light source. The whole file is scenes/sun-room.ts .

 Against three.js at full power

The same scene file, run by both engines on the same Mac. three.js gets everything it has: shadow maps, image-based lighting and, on WebGPU, its own SSGI, SSR and TRAA.

 three.js r187 ThreeRT 
 --- --- 
 
 

 Bistro night, 1280 × 720 Frame cost Error against the reference (ΔE, lower is closer) 
 --- --- ---: 
 ThreeRT, live 15.5 ms (60 fps) 3.4 
 three.js, WebGPU + SSGI + SSR + TRAA 34.7 ms (29 fps) 10.1 
 three.js, WebGL tuned 15.9 ms (60 fps) 12.1 

The reference is an unbiased offline render (4,096 samples per pixel, no denoiser). The method, every scene, and where three.js is ahead (it draws small scenes in about 1 ms) are in docs/COMPARE.md .

 Get started

 Play and make games

1. Download ThreeRT for macOS (14 or later, Apple silicon) or iPhone and iPad (iOS 17 or later). The client fetches a game's code and traces it on the device's own GPU.
2. Open an example from the app's library or from threert.app, where ThreeRT apps and games are published.
3. Write your own with the threert command line that ships inside the Mac app:

 

The same address in any browser shows the game as three.js. The full walk-through is at threert.dev/docs.

 Build your own app on the engine

To put ThreeRT inside a native app of your own, start from the native app templates : one repository with an app per platform in its own UI framework, macOS (SwiftUI) first. It is the recommended way to embed the engine, and it is set up for building with a coding agent:

- a SwiftUI app whose window is a live path-traced view (the engine's LiveCore on a CAMetalLayer , behind a small C ABI), with a sample scene that uses physics, glass, metal and moving lights;
- the Claude Code or Codex already on the machine, in a side panel over the Agent Client Protocol: ask for a change and the agent edits the scene's TypeScript, which the view hot-reloads within a second;
- a code viewer with syntax highlighting that follows the agent's edits, a console, and a scene check / scene shot command line the agent uses to verify its own work.

 

 Packages

 Package What 
 --- --- 
 @threert/scene The three.js-style scene API: meshes, PBR materials, lights, glTF models, physics, volumes 
 @threert/gameplay Games: state, transactional handlers, world handlers, frame scripts; input, a HUD and a channel to the app that runs the game; deterministic and replayable 
 @threert/voxel Destructible voxel levels: explosions, cuts, and pieces that break off as rigid bodies 

 

 threert dev bundles these for you. Install them from npm for types, tests, or a build pipeline of your own.

 Build the engine from source

The engine is Rust and wgpu: hardware ray queries where the GPU has them (Metal, Vulkan), a software BVH where it does not. You need Rust, Node 24 and Bun.

 

In the window: drag to orbit, right-drag to pan, wheel to zoom, WASD/QE to fly, R to reset, P for a snapshot.

 play and live take --quality ( auto , native , quality , balanced , performance , ultra-performance ),
 --reconstruction ( builtin , auto , an upscaler: fsr , metalfx , dlss ; a joint denoiser: metalfx-denoised ,
 dlss-rr ; or a list in order of preference) and --latency . FSR 1 also runs on WebGPU; DLSS requires an opt-in NVIDIA
SDK build; MetalFX requires supported Apple hardware. See
live rendering settings and the TypeScript API.

 

 Demos in this repository

 Demo What Run 
 --- --- --- 
 Light Room A small game: click coins, the floor, the balls, the crate and the walls threert-render play out/bundles/light-room.js 
 Bistro Amazon Lumberyard Bistro at night: a slice, the district, and a crowd of 150 walkers and 60 vans games/bistro-slice , bistro-district , bistro-crowd 
 Zero-Day Beeple's Zero-Day (Measure One), animated games/zero-day 
 Tokyo Shinjuku and Shiba from the PLATEAU city model, with a live time of day games/tokyo , tools/tokyo 
 Voxel level A destructible voxel city: explosions, cuts, whole buildings brought down in pieces, dust and smoke games/voxel-level , docs/VOXEL.md 
 Showreel Light and physics together: glowing balls down a staircase, a wrecking ball through a tower of glowing bricks, 400 lanterns games/showreel 

 Repository layout

 Directory What 
 --- --- 
 renderer/ The engine: the Rust + wgpu path tracer, live viewport, denoiser, post, and an embedded QuickJS that runs scene code ( threert-render ); voxel-core and physics-core (Rapier) also build for wasm32 
 packages/ @threert/scene , @threert/gameplay , @threert/voxel 
 scenes/ , games/ The reference catalog (Cornell box, material grid, Bistro, Zero

install.title: Get started
install.html:
Play and make games
  1. Download ThreeRT for macOS (14 or later, Apple silicon) or iPhone and iPad (iOS 17 or later). The client fetches a game's code and traces it on the device's own GPU.
  2. Open an example from the app's library or from threert.app, where ThreeRT apps and games are published.
  3. Write your own with the threert command line that ships inside the Mac app:
threert create my-game
cd my-game
threert dev        # bundles on save, serves every client on your network, prints a QR code for your phone

The same address in any browser shows the game as three.js. The full walk-through is at threert.dev/docs.

Build your own app on the engine

To put ThreeRT inside a native app of your own, start from the native app templates: one repository with an app per platform in its own UI framework, macOS (SwiftUI) first. It is the recommended way to embed the engine, and it is set up for building with a coding agent:

  • a SwiftUI app whose window is a live path-traced view (the engine's LiveCore on a CAMetalLayer, behind a small C ABI), with a sample scene that uses physics, glass, metal and moving lights;
  • the Claude Code or Codex already on the machine, in a side panel over the Agent Client Protocol: ask for a change and the agent edits the scene's TypeScript, which the view hot-reloads within a second;
  • a code viewer with syntax highlighting that follows the agent's edits, a console, and a scene check / scene shot command line the agent uses to verify its own work.
git clone --recursive https://github.com/threert/native-app-template my-app
cd my-app && bun tools/macos.ts --run
Packages
Package What
@threert/scene The three.js-style scene API: meshes, PBR materials, lights, glTF models, physics, volumes
@threert/gameplay Games: state, transactional handlers, world handlers, frame scripts; input, a HUD and a channel to the app that runs the game; deterministic and replayable
@threert/voxel Destructible voxel levels: explosions, cuts, and pieces that break off as rigid bodies 
npm install @threert/scene @threert/gameplay

threert dev bundles these for you. Install them from npm for types, tests, or a build pipeline of your own.

Build the engine from source

The engine is Rust and wgpu: hardware ray queries where the GPU has them (Metal, Vulkan), a software BVH where it does not. You need Rust, Node 24 and Bun.

npm install && bun scripts/setup.ts      # assets/ -> the machine's shared asset store, then fetch what is missing
node tools/build-scenes.ts                # scenes/*.ts + games -> out/bundles/<id>.js
bun renderer/build.ts                     # -> renderer/target/release/threert-render

renderer/target/release/threert-render play out/bundles/light-room.js                         # a game, in a window
renderer/target/release/threert-render render out/bundles/cornell-box.js -o out/cornell.png --spp 32   # a scene, to an image
node tools/three/open.ts scenes/bistro.ts # the same scene in three.js, in your browser

In the window: drag to orbit, right-drag to pan, wheel to zoom, WASD/QE to fly, R to reset, P for a snapshot.

play and live take --quality (auto, native, quality, balanced, performance, ultra-performance), --reconstruction (builtin, auto, an upscaler: fsr, metalfx, dlss; a joint denoiser: metalfx-denoised, dlss-rr; or a list in order of preference) and --latency. FSR 1 also runs on WebGPU; DLSS requires an opt-in NVIDIA SDK build; MetalFX requires supported Apple hardware. See live rendering settings and the TypeScript API.

npm test && npm run typecheck && (cd renderer && cargo test --release)   # scene API, gameplay, runtime and engine tests
npm run test:render                                                      # the render test suite, on the GPU
